The University of Colorado Boulder publishes her as a Lecturer in its Lockheed Martin Engineering Management Program, previously an adjunct instructor in the Engineering Leadership Program (2022) and Scholar in Residence to the Engineering Management Program (2023). The same page gives her career as a 20-year Naval career as an F/A-18F strike fighter pilot, with combat deployments supporting Operation Iraqi Freedom and Operation Enduring Freedom, a final yearlong assignment as an infrastructure reconstruction engineer in Ghazni, Afghanistan, and a Bronze Star and Air Combat Medal. Prior teaching posts: Naval Science instructor across a Washington DC consortium of Georgetown, George Washington, Howard and Catholic universities, and Military Professor at the US Naval Academy, Department of Leadership, Ethics and Law. Education: BS Civil Engineering, George Washington University; Defense Language Institute certification in Dari; MBA, GW School of Business. This is an employer's published biography of its own lecturer, not a service record.

CBS News, 60 Minutes, correspondent Bill Whitaker, published 16 May 2021, states that Dietrich, a former F/A-18F pilot, 'has never before spoken publicly about what she saw that day'. The same report quotes her: 'It was unidentified. And that's why it was so unsettling to us. Because we weren't expecting it. We couldn't classify it'; 'No predictable movement, no predictable trajectory'; and 'I felt the vulnerability of not having anything to defend ourselves. And then I felt confused when it disappeared.' This dates the start of her public record to 16 May 2021 on the network's own assertion.

In sworn testimony at the 26 July 2023 House Oversight subcommittee hearing, David Fravor placed her in the chain of who re-opened the 2004 case: 'Years later, I was contacted by the other pilot, Alex Dietrich, and asked if I would been contacted and I said no, but I am willing to talk.' Tier 1 for the fact that a sworn witness said this on that date; the underlying sequence is his account.

In sworn testimony at the 13 November 2024 House Oversight joint hearing, Tim Gallaudet named her while alleging AARO pressure on him: 'In addition, they tried to have me question very valid UAP reports like the Tic Tac incident, even coming to a--stating possibly that the Tic Tac was American technology. And then, of course, if you ask David Fravor or Alex Dietrich, the two witnesses, they were convinced it was otherwise.' Tier 1 for the fact that he said it under oath. The allegation about AARO's conduct is his word and caps at Tier 2 as a claim about the world.

label: Alex Dietrich
narrative: Dietrich was the second F/A-18F aircrew on the 14 November 2004 intercept, flying as Fravor's wingman and observing the object for roughly five minutes. She is named alongside Fravor in the Navy's own range fouler report on the incident, released through the Navy FOIA reading room on 13 January 2023 - which matters because it puts her at the event in a government record rather than only in a media account. She stayed silent publicly for sixteen years, then gave her first public account on CBS 60 Minutes on 16 May 2021, opening with 'I never wanted to be on national TV, no offense.' That reluctance is itself the datum: the stigma structure the ODNI's own June 2021 preliminary assessment described - 'disparagement associated with observing UAP, reporting it, or attempting to discuss it with colleagues' - operated on her for a decade and a half. Mike Gold, testifying before House Oversight on 13 November 2024, cited her by name, saying she 'was mocked by her colleagues' and that her incident 'went years without any investigation.' Dietrich has since argued in print for cooperative, data-first investigation rather than advocacy, publishing an opinion piece in The Debrief on 17 February 2023.
